linkedin.body:
A quick one, because it matters more than it sounds.

We have never written "trusted by X businesses" on our own site, and we have labelled all 49 of our portfolio builds as concept projects or sample builds, on the page itself.

That is not humility. It is a decision about what a claim is worth.

A claim is only useful if the buyer can check it. "Trusted by 200+" cannot be checked. It can only be admired, and admiration is where trust goes to die.

If you run a business, the version of this is simple: every number on your page should survive one question. Who is this? Where is the evidence? Can I check it? If the answer is no, it is decoration, and decoration costs you credibility when it is found out.

The same rule applies to the work itself. We would rather look smaller and be believed than look bigger and be doubted.

posts.topic: What a sample project taught us about real customers
posts.why: Story. A specific moment from the work, honestly framed, builds trust without any fake proof.

tiktok.fmt: Talking head over a screen recording, 35s
tiktok.hook: We built a sample restaurant site last month. The hardest part was not the design.
beats: Forty items, no prices, no photos
We had to invent all of it
And that made the design honest
tiktok.vo: We built a sample restaurant site recently. The hardest part was not the design, and it was not the code. It was the menu. A real restaurant has forty items, half of them with photos taken on a phone in bad light, and nobody has written the prices down anywhere. For our sample build we had to invent every item, every price, every description, and that constraint is what made the design honest. If we had been building it for a real restaurant, that conversation would have been the first week of work, not a detail.

facebook.body:
The first question we ask a new client is not about budget. It is not even what they want built.

It is: what changed?

Something changed, or they would not have called us. And when we dig, it is almost always smaller than they expected. It is rarely the website. It is usually that a competitor opened, or a price went up, or a whole batch of people had a bad experience somewhere else entirely.

The website gets the blame because the website is the thing they can see. The real problem is usually somewhere you cannot photograph.

Finding that is the job. The rest is the build.

If you want that answered for your own business, send us your link. Within 24 hours you get a voice note and three points, free, no sales call. WhatsApp: 0905 069 0837.
